**Progress M-14M** (Russian: Прогресс М-14М) was a Russian uncrewed cargo spacecraft that resupplied the **International Space Station (ISS)**. It was part of the **Progress-M** series, which has been a workhorse for ISS logistics since the 1980s. Below is a detailed overview of the mission:

---

### **1. Mission Overview**
- **Spacecraft Type:** Progress-M (11F615A60)
- **Manufacturer:** **RSC Energia** (Russia)
- **Launch Date:** **January 25, 2012, 23:06:40 UTC**
- **Launch Site:** **Baikonur Cosmodrome, Kazakhstan (Site 1/5)**
- **Rocket:** **Soyuz-U**
- **Docking Date:** **January 28, 2012, 00:09 UTC**
- **Docking Port:** **Pirs module (ISS)**
- **Undocking Date:** **April 19, 2012, 11:04 UTC**
- **Deorbit & Reentry:** **April 28, 2012** (burned up over the Pacific Ocean)

---

### **2. Mission Objectives**
Progress M-14M was the **46th Progress mission to the ISS** and had the following primary goals:
- **Resupply the ISS** with food, water, oxygen, fuel, and scientific equipment.
- **Deliver maintenance hardware** for the station.
- **Test new rendezvous and docking systems** (part of Russia’s ongoing upgrades to the Progress fleet).
- **Serve as a trash disposal vehicle** after undocking (burning up on reentry with waste from the ISS).

---

### **3. Payload & Cargo**
The spacecraft carried **2,669 kg (5,884 lbs)** of supplies, including:
- **Dry Cargo (1,260 kg / 2,778 lbs):**
  - Food (including fresh fruits and vegetables)
  - Medical supplies
  - Scientific equipment (experiments for the Russian segment)
  - Clothing and personal items for the crew
  - Tools and spare parts for ISS maintenance
- **Water (420 kg / 926 lbs):**
  - Delivered in **Rodnik tanks** (Russian water supply system).
- **Oxygen & Air (50 kg / 110 lbs):**
  - Used to replenish the station’s atmosphere.
- **Propellant (880 kg / 1,940 lbs):**
  - **Refueling propellant (600 kg / 1,323 lbs)** – Used to reboost the ISS’s orbit.
  - **Propellant for Progress’s own engines (280 kg / 617 lbs)** – Used for maneuvers.

---

### **4. Launch & Rendezvous**
- **Launch Vehicle:** **Soyuz-U** (a reliable workhorse rocket with over 700 successful launches).
- **Trajectory:** The spacecraft followed a **two-day rendezvous profile** (standard at the time; later Progress missions switched to a faster 3-6 hour approach).
- **Docking:** Automated docking to the **Pirs module** using the **Kurs-NA** rendezvous system (an upgraded version of the Kurs system with improved reliability and reduced mass).
- **Crew Monitoring:** The docking was monitored by **Expedition 30** crew members (Anton Shkaplerov, Anatoli Ivanishin, and Oleg Kononenko).

---

### **5. On-Orbit Operations**
- **Duration at ISS:** **82 days** (from docking on January 28 to undocking on April 19, 2012).
- **Activities:**
  - **Cargo Transfer:** The ISS crew unloaded supplies and loaded trash (including used equipment and waste) into the Progress.
  - **Orbital Reboost:** Progress M-14M performed **at least one reboost maneuver** to adjust the ISS’s orbit (counteracting atmospheric drag).
  - **Scientific Experiments:** Some payloads were used for Russian experiments, including **Plasma Crystal-3 Plus** (studying plasma-dust crystals in microgravity).

---

### **6. Undocking & Deorbit**
- **Undocking:** April 19, 2012 – Progress M-14M separated from the **Pirs module** and moved to a safe distance from the ISS.
- **Post-Undocking Tests:**
  - The spacecraft conducted **engine tests** to gather data for future missions.
  - It remained in orbit for **9 days** before deorbiting.
- **Deorbit Burn:** April 28, 2012 – A **retrograde burn** slowed the spacecraft, causing it to reenter the atmosphere.
- **Reentry & Destruction:** The Progress burned up over the **South Pacific Ocean** (a standard disposal zone for Russian spacecraft).

---

### **7. Significance & Legacy**
- **Routine but Critical:** Progress M-14M was one of many resupply missions, but each was essential for keeping the ISS operational.
- **Kurs-NA Testing:** The mission helped validate the **Kurs-NA** system, which was later used on Progress and Soyuz spacecraft.
- **Predecessor to Progress MS:** This mission was part of the **Progress-M** series, which was eventually replaced by the **Progress-MS** (modernized with digital systems, improved docking, and better power efficiency).
- **International Collaboration:** Demonstrated Russia’s key role in ISS logistics, alongside NASA’s Space Shuttle (until 2011) and later commercial providers (SpaceX, Northrop Grumman).

---

### **8. Interesting Facts**
- **Serial Number:** Progress M-14M was also known as **Progress 46P** (the 46th Progress to visit the ISS).
- **No Manual Override Needed:** The docking was fully automated, though the crew could take manual control if needed.
- **Trash Disposal:** The Progress carried **~1,000 kg (2,200 lbs) of waste** from the ISS when it deorbited.
- **Soyuz-U’s Reliability:** The Soyuz-U rocket used for this launch had a **97% success rate** over its lifetime (retired in 2017).

---

### **9. Related Missions**
- **Previous Mission:** **Progress M-13M** (launched October 2011, docked to Pirs).
- **Next Mission:** **Progress M-15M** (launched April 2012, tested a new Kurs-NA system).
- **Soyuz TMA-03M:** The crew that monitored Progress M-14M’s docking (Expedition 30) arrived on this Soyuz.

---

### **10. Media & Documentation**
- **NASA TV Coverage:** The docking was broadcast live on NASA TV.
- **Roscosmos Press Releases:** Provided updates on the mission (available in Russian).
- **Photos & Videos:**
  - [NASA’s Progress M-14M Gallery](https://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/station/structure/elements/progress.html)
  - [Roscosmos Progress M-14M Page (Russian)](http://www.roscosmos.ru/)

---

### **Conclusion**
Progress M-14M was a **routine but vital resupply mission** that ensured the ISS had the necessary supplies for its crew. While not as high-profile as crewed missions, Progress spacecraft like M-14M have been the **backbone of ISS logistics** for decades. The mission also contributed to the **evolution of Russian docking systems**, paving the way for future upgrades.
